note.text: Reading involves following what a passage states, connecting its ideas and distinguishing supported inference from invention. Identify the main idea and locate evidence for each answer. A question may concern a detail, reason, sequence or word in context. If the text omits information, do not supply an invented fact. A plausible outcome is not necessarily a reported result.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to compare the passage’s trading arrangements and interpret its vocabulary without assuming unreported prices or outcomes. Builds on: context clues, collocations and reasoned comparison. Leads to: argumentative writing and checking claims about transactions.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: An imaginary Douala seller displays goods online and at a stall. An online customer asks about the item, total price and delivery before deciding. A stall customer can inspect the displayed item but still needs clear information. The seller keeps a transaction record. Online ordering can extend contact beyond the stall, yet a listing alone proves neither product quality nor guaranteed delivery. No actual price or platform is named.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Read the whole passage before answering. Point to a phrase supporting the answer and explain any inference. When summarising, preserve who did what and whether an action was planned or completed. These original classroom texts are not extracts from prescribed literature.

No: any unrelated opinion replaces the main idea.
No: a summary must be longer than every source text.
e: A summary does not invent a resolution.
An unrelated opinion is not a faithful summary.
Length alone is not the criterion.
